The GfS+ scoring method

Source: vignettes/gfs-scoring.Rmd
gfs-scoring.Rmd

What this answers. How one question becomes a GfS+ point score, and which rule applies to each question type.

What you need. A .qsf, or a question catalogue (see vignette("extensions")).

What to keep in mind. Scores are per question and per loop iteration, and routing is applied later. The rules map each question onto the published scheme, which weighs response tasks by type and complexity. A few Table 1 weights apply only when you set them by hand.

For how scores combine across the survey’s paths see vignette("paths-and-display-logic"). For reading the finished report see vignette("reading-the-report").

library(surveyBurden)
#> 
#>                   .-- Q2 -- Q3 --.
#>   survey -- Q1 --+               +-- Burden 0.3.0
#>                   '-- Q4 --------'
#> 
#> Measuring the Response Burden of Web Surveys
#> Docs: https://pmpk20.github.io/surveyBurden/
#> 
#> Please cite: King P (2026). surveyBurden: Measuring the Response Burden
#> of Web Surveys. R package version 0.3.0,
#> https://github.com/pmpk20/surveyBurden.
#> Use citation("surveyBurden") for BibTeX.
demo <- system.file("extdata", "demo_travel_survey.qsf", package = "surveyBurden")
qsf <- read_qsf(demo)
catalogue <- parse_qsf(qsf)

Where the scheme comes from

GfS stands for Gesellschaft für Sozialforschung (Society for Social Research), a Zürich organisation that used a point system to budget face-to-face interviews. Axhausen and colleagues adapted it to self-administered surveys. Each question earns points by its type and complexity, and the points are added up, so longer or more complex surveys score higher (Schmid and Axhausen 2019). The survey literature calls this kind of measure objective burden, the work a survey asks of respondents measured from the questions themselves (Yan and Williams 2022).

surveyBurden transcribes the current table (Heimgartner and Axhausen 2024, Table 1) verbatim into gfs_scheme(). It adds documented rules for Qualtrics question types that the table lacks, hence GfS+.

w <- gfs_scheme()
w$yes_no
#> [1] 1
w$rating_small
#> [1] 2
w$rating_large
#> [1] 3
w$points_per_minute
#> [1] 12

A few of the Table 1 weights, in points per response action:

response action GfS+ points
yes / no question 1
rating scale, up to 5 options 2
rating scale, more than 5 options 3
first answer to an open question 6
two-alternative stated-choice task 2, plus 1 per attribute (declared tasks only, see below)

Heimgartner and Axhausen (2024) give the full table. gfs_scheme() holds every Table 1 weight, and the automatic scorer uses most of them. What the automatic scorer applies lists which.

Classification first

classify_question() maps each Qualtrics widget to a standard question type. It reads the widget’s selector and options as well as its type, because one MC widget can be a yes/no item, a rating scale, a dropdown or a multi-select.

table(catalogue$std_type)
#> 
#>   descriptive        matrix  multi_choice     open_text single_choice 
#>             1             4             1             3            17

Three layers

score_burden() then works in three layers.

  1. What Qualtrics says the widget is (for example MC with a dropdown selector).
  2. What response action that implies (choose one value from an ordered list).
  3. Which Table 1 category best represents that action (a rating).

Where the structure fixes step 3 (a two-option choice is a closed yes/no item whatever it asks), the mapping is deterministic and the score is marked auto. Where the scheme needs something the .qsf lacks, the package applies an explicit, documented inference rule and marks the item inferred. Every scored question carries a score_basis string recording the rule applied.

scored <- score_burden(catalogue, scheme = w)
table(scored$score_flag)
#> 
#>     auto inferred 
#>       19        7
head(scored[order(-scored$gfs_points),
            c("question_id", "std_type", "gfs_points", "score_flag", "score_basis")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   question_id std_type     gfs_points score_flag score_basis                    
#>   <chr>       <chr>             <dbl> <chr>      <chr>                          
#> 1 QID21       matrix               18 auto       matrix, 6 rows x GfS rating >5…
#> 2 QID19       matrix               14 auto       matrix, 7 rows x GfS rating <=…
#> 3 QID14       multi_choice         12 auto       multi-select, 6 options -> GfS…
#> 4 QID20       matrix               12 auto       matrix, 6 rows x GfS rating <=…
#> 5 QID1        descriptive          11 inferred   transition/instruction text: 1…
#> 6 QID7        matrix                8 auto       matrix, 4 rows x GfS rating <=…

score_flag takes four values.

  • auto means the structure fixes the GfS+ mapping.
  • inferred means the structure is clear and choosing the Table 1 category took an explicit judgement (a dropdown mapped to “rating” as the closest category, a numeric-looking dropdown mapped to “simple numerical answer”, a slider). The number is still determinate.
  • manual means the mapping is uncertain and a person should check it.
  • unknown marks an unmapped type, left unscored as NA. A survey with unknown types is under-counted, and burden_report() warns about it.

The flags separate GfS-native quantities, which the original scheme specifies (question type, response action, number of alternatives), from package-derived ones, which the package estimates because the .qsf lacks them (line counts, response-unit structure).

Documented inference rules for gaps in Table 1

  • Instruction-text lines. Table 1 counts rendered lines of instruction text. A .qsf stores words, so the package estimates lines as words / words_per_line (default 12). This is a practical conversion that you can override with burden_report(words_per_line = ...). See vignette("calibration").
  • Dropdowns (MC with a DL selector) lack a Table 1 row. They score as a rating (2.0 for up to 5 options, 3.0 for more), or as a simple numerical answer (1.0) when the options are numbers and the question asks for a quantity or a date.
  • Sliders also lack a Table 1 row. They score as a numerical answer when the axis label carries units, and as a rating otherwise.
  • Hidden questions. A question hidden from the respondent by injected CSS or JavaScript scores 0.
  • Loop & Merge blocks. Item scores are per iteration, and the multiplication happens later, when paths are scored. The structural profile spreads each loop’s iteration count evenly from 1 to the block’s explicit cap. The naive ceiling uses the cap and the naive floor one iteration. A loop without an explicit cap counts its questions once, which can understate the upper figures. Display logic inside a loop is evaluated in each iteration (see vignette("paths-and-display-logic")).

Question stems

Table 1’s “question or transition, up to 3 lines = 2.0” applies to standalone instruction blocks only. The question text itself earns no separate points, because the GfS scheme leaves unclear whether a question’s reading cost belongs in the item weight or on its own. A question with a long stem is therefore scored conservatively, and its stem length appears separately as a readability diagnostic (see vignette("reading-the-report")).

Multi-answer matrices

Table 1 has no rule for a grid where each cell allows several answers (“tick all that apply” across two axes). surveyBurden scores it as rows x cols x 0.5. Each cell is one simple yes/no decision, which GfS scores at 1.0, discounted here because answering in a grid takes less working memory. The formula is symmetric in rows and columns, so the score stays the same however Qualtrics stored the grid. This rule is a GfS+ extension, and its weight is gfs_scheme()$matrix_cell_multi.

What the automatic scorer applies

Each standard question type gets one rule. This table is the complete list, and score_basis names the rule used for each question.

Question type (std_type) Automatic rule Scheme entries used Flag
single_choice, 2 options closed yes/no yes_no auto
single_choice, 3-5 / 6+ options rating rating_small / rating_large auto
single_choice, option count unknown assumed a rating up to 5 rating_small inferred
dropdown rating by option count, or a simple numerical answer when the options are numbers and the question asks for a quantity or date rating_small, rating_large, numeric_answer inferred
multi_choice, n options half-open: base + per extra option, switching at multi_large_threshold multi_small_*, multi_large_* auto
matrix, single answer per row rows x rating by column count rating_small / rating_large auto
matrix, multiple answers per row rows x cols x cell weight matrix_cell_multi inferred
open_text, single line answer of up to 5 words open_short auto
open_text, multi-line first answer to an open question open_essay auto
slider numerical answer when the label has units, else a rating numeric_answer, slider inferred
ranking best-of ranking, first item only rank_base auto
constant_sum numerical answer numeric_answer inferred
descriptive base + per line beyond 3, lines = words / words_per_line descriptive_*, words_per_line auto
captcha fixed small cost captcha auto
timing, meta, or hidden by CSS/JS 0 auto / inferred
anything else left as NA, counted as 0 in totals unknown

Stated-choice tasks. A QSF stores a choice task as an ordinary widget, so the scorer treats it as that widget (usually a single choice). Declare your tasks with choice_tasks, a data frame of question_id, n_alternatives and n_attributes, in burden_report() or any other burden function. Each declared task scores 2 points for two alternatives, 3 for three and 1 more for each alternative beyond three (an extrapolation past Table 1), plus 1 per attribute (sc_per_variable). Count an opt-out such as “neither” as an alternative. suggest_choice_tasks() lists questions that look like choice tasks (an HTML table in the stem) for you to check before you declare them.

Filter and branching points. GfS adds 0.5 for a filter and 0.5 for a branching. GfS budgets interviewer-administered surveys, where the interviewer applies each filter. In a web survey the software applies them, so these points are off by default (apply_filter_branching = FALSE). Set s$apply_filter_branching <- TRUE to match a manual GfS count. A question then earns 0.5 if its answer drives another question’s display logic and 0.5 if a flow branch tests it. Embedded data fields, randomiser assignments and Displayed conditions earn nothing.

Reference-only entries. gfs_scheme() holds these Table 1 weights for completeness, and no automatic rule reads them, so changing them leaves every score the same. They are rank_per_item, open_medium, please_specify and open_essay_per_extra. In practice:

  • a ranking scores its first item only, so rankings of several items are under-scored;
  • “please specify” boxes and repeated open answers score as the widget Qualtrics used for them (a text box).

Where your survey has these, check the affected questions’ score_basis and adjust by hand if needed.

What can make the reported figures too low. Unscored (unknown) questions contribute 0, loops without an explicit cap count once, and the reference-only items above are under-scored. burden_report() warns about unscored questions, and calculation_certainty() counts loops with unknown caps.

Overriding the weights

You can change any weight in gfs_scheme() and pass the scheme back in. Only the entries a rule uses (table above) affect scores.

w2 <- gfs_scheme()
w2$rating_small <- 2.5
score_burden(catalogue, scheme = w2)$gfs_points[1:5]
#> [1] 11.0  1.0  2.5  1.0  2.5
